facts.title: A Symbol From Latin
facts.text: Iron's chemical symbol Fe comes from its Latin name, ferrum. The English word 'iron' descends from Old English isern and Proto-Germanic isarnan, words that predate written records. This split between a Germanic common name and a Latin scientific symbol is why the abbreviation looks nothing like the spoken word.

facts.title: Older Than Smelting
facts.text: Long before humans learned to smelt ore around 1200 BCE, ancient Egyptians crafted iron beads from meteorites. Beads found at Gerzeh and dated to about 3200 BCE were hammered from nickel-rich meteoric iron, which is why the Egyptians sometimes called iron 'metal of heaven.' These are among the oldest known iron artifacts on Earth.

facts.title: The Cosmic Dead End
facts.text: Iron sits at a special peak in nuclear binding energy: its isotope iron-56 is among the most tightly bound nuclei that exist. This means a massive star cannot release energy by fusing iron, so when its core turns to iron, fusion stops and the star collapses, triggering a supernova. Iron is effectively the ash of stellar fusion.

facts.title: The Reason Blood Is Red
facts.text: Each molecule of hemoglobin in your red blood cells contains four iron atoms, and each can grab one oxygen molecule for transport around the body. An average adult carries roughly 3 to 4 grams of iron, most of it locked inside this protein. The interaction of light with the iron-bearing heme group is what gives oxygen-rich blood its bright red color.

facts.title: Earth's Molten Heart
facts.text: Iron is the most abundant element on Earth by mass, largely because the planet's core is mostly iron mixed with some nickel. The solid inner core and liquid outer core are made of this metal, and churning currents in the molten outer core generate Earth's magnetic field. That field deflects harmful solar radiation and lets compasses point north.

facts.title: Rust Never Sleeps
facts.text: When iron meets oxygen and water, it forms hydrated iron oxides we call rust. Unlike the protective oxide layer on aluminum, rust is flaky and porous, so it keeps exposing fresh metal and eats steadily into the metal. Corrosion of iron and steel costs the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars every year.

facts.title: Curie's Magnetic Limit
facts.text: Iron is one of only a few elements that are ferromagnetic, meaning it can become a permanent magnet at room temperature. But heat destroys this property: above its Curie temperature of 770 degrees Celsius, iron loses its magnetism entirely. Cool it back down and the magnetic ordering returns.

facts.title: From Iron To Steel
facts.text: Pure iron is actually fairly soft; its strength as a building material comes from alloying it with carbon to make steel. Adding less than 2 percent carbon dramatically increases hardness, and steel is now produced at well over a billion tonnes per year. This alloy underpins skyscrapers, ships, cars, and railways worldwide.

facts.title: The Red Planet's Coat
facts.text: Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide dust, essentially the same rust that forms on Earth. Iron is also common in asteroids and meteorites, and iron-nickel meteorites provided some of humanity's earliest usable metal. The element is one of the most abundant in the universe, forged inside stars.

facts.title: Shape-Shifting Crystals
facts.text: Solid iron does not keep one fixed atomic arrangement; it changes its crystal structure as it heats. Below 912 degrees Celsius it is body-centered cubic (called ferrite), then it switches to a face-centered cubic form (austenite) at higher temperatures. Metallurgists exploit these transformations, along with rapid cooling, to control the hardness and toughness of steel.
